But I would ask further, as I ask now: "Is there anything in Judge Cohalan's reply that would manifest even a consent to co-operate with De Valera, or with Ireland herself in the person of her representative?"is there not, on the contrary, evidence of a decided prejudice and a preconceived determinaation to resist -- not to say thwart cooperation on the part of the F.O.I.F .? In other words, does not the judge, in said reply to DeValera speak for himself and his constituents as really more an American Pro- tective Association than as the F.O. I.F. is defined -- "an association of American citizens founded to assist the Irish people in securing freedom for the Irish people?" How, then, can anyone blame the repre- sentative of the Island of Saints and Sages for refusing, even "to dis- cuss the question" of a compromise with such leaders of a society whose rank and file members would be justly indignant at the very insinuation, though in all truth they might be called real "A.P.A's" instead of Friends of Ireland? Their fear of danger from Ireland's alliance with England would be, or is, just about as reasonable as the fear of the original A.P.A. from an alliance of the Pope with the professed powers of Hell -- just as affected, too. As to DeValera's "Cuban blunder," well, DeValera's every utterance ever since, not to say his every action, including his tragic return to Ireland, seals that as an evident calumny. Talk about "splitters," as long the objective is practically iden- tical sounds to me like so much wind. The splitters -- would-be or other- wise -- in any great cause are those who for selfish motives swerve from first principles, even as the real greatness of any nation --- republic or other -- may be measured by the pervading spirit of national righteousness which, by the way, considering our governmental silence these many moons regarding British and allied outrages, etc, is not saying much for the "greatest republic." Of course, if the F.O. I.F. is the fruit of any one's personal gen- ius, and therefore liable to be claimed as personal property, nobody can blame such genius for frothing a little when a stranger refuses to ac- knowledge his right, but if, as quite a few of us believe, such societie are divinely providential then the more and the longer such a "genius" frothes the more ridiculous and the more pitiable -- not to say contempti- ble he makes himself.
